title: AI, ML, deep learning and generative AI
body:
The terms nest inside each other:

- Artificial intelligence (AI): systems that perform tasks that normally need human intelligence.
- Machine learning (ML): the part of AI where a model learns patterns from data instead of following hand-written rules.
- Deep learning: ML with neural networks of many layers; it handles unstructured data such as images, audio and text.
- Generative AI: deep learning models, usually foundation models, that create new content (text, images, code, audio).
- Agentic AI: systems where a model plans steps and calls tools to reach a goal.

Training builds a model from data; inference uses the trained model to make predictions on new data.

Read more: https://aws.amazon.com/what-is/deep-learning/
commonMistakes: Treating deep learning and generative AI as synonyms: generative AI is one use of deep learning.
Calling a rules engine written by experts "machine learning": nothing is learned from data.

title: Supervised, unsupervised and reinforcement learning
body:
- Supervised learning: every training example has a known answer (label). Used for classification and regression.
- Unsupervised learning: no labels; the model finds structure, such as clusters or anomalies.
- Semi-supervised learning: a small labeled set plus a large unlabeled set.
- Reinforcement learning: an agent takes actions in an environment and learns from rewards and penalties.
- Self-supervised learning: the data provides its own labels (for example, predicting the next word), which is how foundation models are pre-trained.

Read more: https://aws.amazon.com/compare/the-difference-between-machine-learning-supervised-and-unsupervised/
commonMistakes: Picking reinforcement learning whenever the word "feedback" appears: labeled history is supervised learning.
Assuming unsupervised learning can predict a known target: it has no target to learn.

title: Regression, classification and clustering
body:
- Regression predicts a continuous number: a price, a temperature, minutes until delivery.
- Binary classification picks one of two classes (spam or not); multiclass picks one of several.
- Clustering groups similar items without predefined labels (customer segments); k-means is a common algorithm.
- Forecasting predicts future values of a time series.
- Anomaly detection flags unusual records, such as fraud.

Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/sagemaker/latest/dg/autopilot-datasets-problem-types.html
commonMistakes: Calling a numeric prediction "classification" because the number is later put into bands.
Using clustering when labeled examples exist and the goal is to predict a known class.

title: SageMaker AI inference options
body:
- Real-time inference: a persistent endpoint for low-latency, interactive requests.
- Serverless Inference: no instances to choose; scales with traffic and to zero; suits intermittent traffic that tolerates cold starts. No GPUs.
- Asynchronous Inference: queues requests with large payloads (up to 1 GB) and long processing (up to one hour); can scale to zero when idle.
- Batch Transform: offline inference over a whole dataset in Amazon S3; no endpoint stays running.

Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/sagemaker/latest/dg/deploy-model.html
commonMistakes: Choosing a real-time endpoint for a nightly job: it bills while idle all day.
Choosing Serverless Inference for GPU models or minutes-long requests.

title: AWS managed AI services
body:
Pretrained services you call through an API, no ML expertise needed:

- Amazon Transcribe: speech to text.
- Amazon Polly: text to speech.
- Amazon Translate: translation between languages.
- Amazon Comprehend: NLP on text: sentiment, entities, key phrases, PII, topics.
- Amazon Lex: chatbots and voice bots (conversational interfaces).
- Amazon Rekognition: image and video analysis.
- Amazon Textract: text, forms and tables from documents.
- Amazon SageMaker AI: build, train and deploy your own models.

Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/comprehend/latest/dg/what-is.html
commonMistakes: Mixing up Polly (text to speech) and Transcribe (speech to text).
Expecting Translate or Lex to score sentiment: that is Comprehend.

title: When to use ML, traditional ML or a foundation model
body:
ML adds value for decisions at scale, automation and patterns too complex for rules. It is a poor fit when the rules are known and an exact, deterministic result is required, or when the cost outweighs the benefit.

Traditional ML (for example, gradient-boosted trees on tabular data) suits structured data, tight cost or latency limits and strict explainability or regulatory requirements. Foundation models suit open-ended language, image and multimodal tasks where a pretrained model saves building one.

Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/aws-certification/latest/ai-practitioner-01/ai-practitioner-01-domain1.html
commonMistakes: Reaching for a foundation model for a calculation with a published formula.
Treating text an LLM writes about its decision as a faithful explanation of it.

title: The ML lifecycle on AWS
body:
Stages and the SageMaker AI features that support them:

- Collect and label data: SageMaker Ground Truth (human labeling).
- Prepare data and features: SageMaker Data Wrangler, Feature Store.
- Train and tune: training jobs, automatic model tuning; Debugger watches training.
- Evaluate and check bias: SageMaker Clarify.
- Deploy: endpoints, Batch Transform.
- Monitor: SageMaker Model Monitor detects data and model quality drift against a baseline.
- Automate (MLOps): SageMaker Pipelines, Model Registry; retrain when monitoring shows drift.

Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/sagemaker/latest/dg/model-monitor.html
commonMistakes: Using Model Monitor for labeling or Ground Truth for production monitoring.
Expecting endpoint latency metrics to reveal data drift.

title: Model performance metrics
body:
For classification, from the confusion matrix:

- Accuracy: share of all predictions that are right. Misleading on imbalanced data.
- Precision: of the items flagged positive, how many really are. Matters when false positives are costly.
- Recall: of the real positives, how many were found. Matters when missing a case is costly.
- F1 score: harmonic mean of precision and recall.
- AUC: how well the model ranks positives above negatives across thresholds.

For regression: RMSE, MAE, R². Business metrics (cost per user, ROI, customer feedback) judge whether the model is worth it.

Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/sagemaker/latest/dg/autopilot-metrics-validation.html
commonMistakes: Trusting 99% accuracy on a dataset where 99% of records are negative.
Mixing up precision (false positives) and recall (false negatives).

title: Types of data in AI models
body:
- Labeled data carries the answer (the target) for each example and is needed for supervised learning; unlabeled data has no answer and suits unsupervised learning.
- Structured (tabular) data fits rows and columns: numbers, short text, dates, as in a relational table or spreadsheet.
- Unstructured data does not fit a table: free text, images, audio and video.
- Time-series data is a sequence of values ordered by time, such as hourly sensor readings or daily sales, and is used for forecasting.
- Image data feeds computer vision; text data feeds natural language processing.

Read more: https://aws.amazon.com/compare/the-difference-between-structured-data-and-unstructured-data/
commonMistakes: Calling free-text reviews structured because they are stored in a database column.
Assuming unlabeled data can train a model to predict a known target.

title: Real-world AI applications and where they add value
body:
AI and ML add value by assisting human decisions (ranking claims for review), by scaling a task to volumes people cannot handle, and by automating repetitive work.

Common applications and an AWS fit:

- Computer vision: Amazon Rekognition; documents: Amazon Textract.
- NLP: Amazon Comprehend; translation: Amazon Translate.
- Speech recognition: Amazon Transcribe; speech output: Amazon Polly; chat and voice bots: Amazon Lex.
- Recommendations: Amazon Personalize.
- Fraud and anomaly detection, forecasting: models built in Amazon SageMaker AI.
- Knowledge bases: Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases.
- Agentic AI: agents that plan and call tools, built with Amazon Bedrock and AgentCore.

Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/personalize/latest/dg/what-is-personalize.html
commonMistakes: Using a document search service for personalized recommendations.
Calling a fixed rule written by people an AI application.

title: MLOps on SageMaker AI
body:
MLOps applies engineering practice to ML so models reach production and stay healthy:

- Experimentation: managed MLflow on SageMaker AI logs each run's parameters and metrics for comparison.
- Repeatable processes: SageMaker Pipelines runs data preparation, training, evaluation and registration the same way every time.
- Versioning and approval: SageMaker Model Registry catalogs model versions and their approval status.
- Monitoring: SageMaker Model Monitor detects data and model quality drift against a baseline.
- Re-training: a drift alert can start a pipeline that retrains and registers a new version for approval.
- Managing technical debt: avoid one-off notebooks and manual steps that nobody can reproduce.

Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/sagemaker/latest/dg/pipelines.html
commonMistakes: Treating Model Registry as an orchestrator: Pipelines runs the steps, the registry stores the versions.
Retraining on a fixed schedule with no monitoring signal and no approval step.

title: Where models come from and the AWS tools around them
body:
Sources of foundation models:

- Managed API: Amazon Bedrock serves provider models without exposing their weights; providers cannot see customer prompts.
- Open-weight pretrained models: SageMaker JumpStart deploys and fine-tunes them on instances in your own account (self-hosted).
- Custom models: training from scratch needs very large datasets and compute; most teams start from a pretrained model.

Tools for each stage:

- Amazon SageMaker AI: build, train, deploy and monitor ML models.
- Amazon Bedrock: build generative AI applications and agents on foundation models.
- Kiro: an AI-powered development environment; specs turn a feature into requirements, design and tasks.
- Amazon Quick: an AI workspace for business users with dashboards (Quick Sight), research, flows and chat over company data.

Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/quick/latest/userguide/what-is.html
commonMistakes: Expecting to download the weights of a model used through Bedrock.
Mixing up Kiro (for developers) and Amazon Quick (for business users).

title: Generative AI building blocks
body:
- Token: the unit of text a model reads and writes (roughly a word piece). Pricing and context limits count tokens.
- Context window: the maximum tokens a model can take in one request.
- Embedding: a vector of numbers that captures meaning; similar content sits close together.
- Vector store: a database that indexes embeddings for similarity search.
- Chunking: splitting documents into pieces before embedding them.
- Transformer: the neural network architecture behind LLMs; attention lets it weigh every token against the others.
- Foundation model (FM): a large model pre-trained on broad data and adapted to many tasks.
- Diffusion model: generates images by removing noise step by step.
- Multimodal model: takes or produces more than one type of data, such as text and images.

Read more: https://aws.amazon.com/what-is/embeddings-in-machine-learning/
commonMistakes: Thinking embeddings are a compressed copy you can turn back into the original text.
Confusing a keyword index with semantic (vector) search.

title: Limits of generative AI
body:
Advantages: adaptability, natural conversation, fast content creation.

Disadvantages:

- Hallucination: confident output that is false or not grounded in a source.
- Nondeterminism: the same prompt can give different outputs, because tokens are sampled.
- Interpretability: it is hard to see why a model produced an output.
- Inaccuracy and knowledge cutoff: the model knows only its training data unless given more context.

Mitigations: grounding with RAG, lower temperature, guardrails, human review, evaluation.

Read more: https://aws.amazon.com/what-is/generative-ai/
commonMistakes: Calling any unexpected output a hallucination: varied but correct wording is nondeterminism.
Believing temperature 0 guarantees identical output in every case.

title: Choosing a model and measuring its value
body:
Selection criteria: task and modality, quality on your own evaluation set, latency, cost per token, context window and input/output length, languages, customization options, compliance and Region availability. The smallest model that meets the quality bar is usually the best choice.

Measure value with business metrics, not only technical scores: conversion rate, average revenue per user, customer lifetime value, efficiency, task completion, ROI.

Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/evaluation.html
commonMistakes: Assuming the largest model is always the right one.
Reporting BLEU or token counts when the question is business impact.

title: Amazon Bedrock pricing and cost levers
body:
- On-demand: pay per input and output token (per image for image models). No commitment.
- Batch inference: submit many prompts in files in Amazon S3; results are written back to S3. For supported models, 50% lower price than on-demand.
- Provisioned Throughput: reserved capacity billed by the hour; commitment terms lower the rate. Required for some custom models.
- Prompt caching: reuse a repeated prompt prefix to cut input token cost and latency.
- Cross-Region inference: spreads requests across Regions for throughput. Geographic profiles keep processing within a geography; global profiles can route worldwide and are priced separately.

Read more: https://aws.amazon.com/bedrock/pricing/
commonMistakes: Buying Provisioned Throughput for a job that runs a few hours a day.
Expecting lower temperature or shorter output to cut the cost of a long repeated input.

title: AWS services for building generative AI
body:
- Amazon Bedrock: fully managed access to foundation models from Amazon and other providers through one API; knowledge bases, agents, guardrails, evaluations, customization. No servers to manage.
- Amazon SageMaker AI and SageMaker JumpStart: deploy, fine-tune or train models (including open-weight FMs) on instances you choose, with full control.
- Amazon Bedrock AgentCore: services to run, secure and operate agents in production (runtime, gateway, identity, memory, observability).
- Amazon Q: generative AI assistants for business users and developers.

Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/what-is-bedrock.html
commonMistakes: Expecting to download base model weights from Bedrock.
Choosing Bedrock when the requirement is to pick instance types and manage the endpoint.

title: Agents, tools and MCP
body:
An AI agent uses a foundation model to plan steps toward a goal, call tools (APIs, functions, knowledge bases), keep memory between steps and decide when it is done.

- Amazon Bedrock Agents: define action groups (API schemas or Lambda functions) and knowledge bases the agent can use.
- Model Context Protocol (MCP): an open standard for connecting agents to tools and data sources. AgentCore Gateway turns APIs and Lambda functions into MCP tools.
- Agent2Agent (A2A): a protocol for agents to communicate with each other.
- Multi-agent patterns: a supervisor agent routes work to specialist agents.

Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/agents.html
commonMistakes: Expecting a knowledge base alone to take actions: it only retrieves.
Mixing up MCP (agent to tool) and A2A (agent to agent).

title: Inference parameters
body:
- Temperature: randomness of token choice. Lower is more focused and consistent; higher is more varied and creative.
- Top P: sample only from the most likely tokens whose probabilities add up to P. Lower is more focused.
- Top K: sample only from the K most likely tokens.
- Maximum tokens (response length): caps the output; output is cut off when reached.
- Stop sequences: strings that end generation.

Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/inference-parameters.html
commonMistakes: Raising temperature to get more consistent answers: it does the opposite.
Expecting max tokens to make answers more accurate rather than just shorter.

title: RAG and Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases
body:
Retrieval augmented generation (RAG) retrieves relevant passages from your data at question time and adds them to the prompt, so answers use current, private information without retraining.

Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases manage the pipeline: ingest documents from a data source, chunk them, create embeddings, store them in a vector store, and retrieve them for each query, with citations.

Supported vector stores include Amazon OpenSearch Serverless, Amazon OpenSearch Service managed clusters, Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL, Amazon Neptune Analytics and Amazon S3 Vectors, plus some third-party stores.

Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/knowledge-base.html
commonMistakes: Fine-tuning to add facts that change weekly: RAG picks them up on the next sync.
Assuming any database is a supported knowledge base vector store.

title: Prompt engineering techniques
body:
A prompt can hold instructions, context, input data and an output format. Techniques:

- Zero-shot: the task with no examples.
- Single-shot (one-shot): one example.
- Few-shot: several examples of input and expected output.
- Chain-of-thought: ask the model to reason step by step before answering.
- Prompt templates: reusable prompts with variables.
- Negative prompts: say what to leave out (common for image models).

Best practice: be specific and concise, give context, state the format, experiment and compare. Amazon Bedrock Prompt Management stores prompts, compares variants and keeps versions.

Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/design-a-prompt.html
commonMistakes: Calling a prompt with one example "few-shot".
Jumping to fine-tuning before trying few-shot prompts.

title: Prompt attacks and other prompt risks
body:
- Prompt injection: input that inserts instructions to override the developer's, possibly hidden in retrieved content.
- Hijacking: making the model pursue a different goal or persona.
- Jailbreaking: prompts designed to bypass the model's safety controls.
- Exposure (leaking): extracting the system prompt or confidential data.
- Poisoning: corrupting training or retrieval data so the model learns or repeats bad content.

Amazon Bedrock Guardrails has a prompt attack filter; tag user input so it is checked separately from the system prompt.

Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/guardrails-prompt-attack.html
commonMistakes: Calling a run-time prompt attack "poisoning": poisoning targets data.
Relying on a polite instruction in the system prompt as the only defense.

title: Customizing a foundation model
body:
Roughly in order of effort:

- Prompt engineering and in-context (few-shot) learning: no training.
- RAG: no training; adds current or private knowledge at query time.
- Supervised fine-tuning: train on labeled prompt and response pairs to improve a specific task; produces a custom model.
- Reinforcement fine-tuning: improve a model with reward functions that score its responses, instead of labeled pairs.
- Continued pre-training: train on large amounts of unlabeled domain text to adapt to a domain's language.
- Distillation: train a smaller student model from a larger teacher model's responses, for lower cost and latency.
- Pre-training from scratch: the most data and compute.

RLHF (reinforcement learning from human feedback) aligns a model with human preferences.

Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/custom-models.html
commonMistakes: Fine-tuning without labeled pairs: unlabeled text calls for continued pre-training.
Expecting fine-tuning a large model to make it cheaper to run: distill to a smaller one.

title: Evaluating foundation models
body:
- Automatic metrics: ROUGE (n-gram overlap with references, summarization), BLEU (n-gram precision, translation), BERTScore (meaning, via embeddings), accuracy, robustness, toxicity.
- LLM-as-a-judge: a second model scores responses against criteria.
- Human evaluation: people rate subjective qualities such as tone or helpfulness.
- Benchmark datasets: standard test sets for comparing models.

Amazon Bedrock evaluations run automatic, judge-model and human-worker evaluation jobs for models, knowledge bases and RAG applications. Business alignment is measured separately: task completion rate, user satisfaction, cost per interaction.

Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/sagemaker/latest/dg/clarify-foundation-model-evaluate-overview.html
commonMistakes: Using BLEU for summarization when the requirement is recall of reference content (ROUGE).
Using Guardrails to compare models: they filter content, they do not score models.

title: Amazon Bedrock Guardrails
body:
Configurable safeguards applied to prompts and responses:

- Content filters: hate, insults, sexual, violence, misconduct, and prompt attacks.
- Denied topics: subjects the application must not discuss.
- Word filters: block specific words or phrases.
- Sensitive information filters: detect PII and custom patterns; block the message or mask the values.
- Contextual grounding check: scores responses for grounding in the source and relevance to the query, to filter hallucinations.
- Automated Reasoning checks: validate responses against formal rules.

Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/guardrails.html
commonMistakes: Using a denied topic when the need is to mask individual values: use a sensitive information filter.
Expecting AWS WAF or Macie to filter model output.

title: Bias, variance and representative data
body:
- Underfitting (high bias): too simple; poor on training and new data.
- Overfitting (high variance): fits training data closely, generalizes poorly. Fix with more data, regularization, simpler models, early stopping.
- Dataset bias: groups that are underrepresented or mislabeled lead to worse results for those groups.

Good datasets are diverse, inclusive, balanced and curated. Detect problems with subgroup analysis, label-quality checks and human audits. Removing a sensitive attribute does not remove proxies for it.

Read more: https://aws.amazon.com/what-is/overfitting/
commonMistakes: Calling a train/test gap from the same period "data drift".
Deleting the sensitive column and assuming the bias is gone.

title: Tools for responsible AI on AWS
body:
- Amazon SageMaker Clarify: pre-training bias metrics on data, post-training bias metrics on predictions, and SHAP explanations; also evaluates foundation models.
- Amazon Augmented AI (Amazon A2I): human review of predictions that meet conditions, such as low confidence.
- Amazon SageMaker Model Monitor: watches bias and quality drift in production.
- Amazon Bedrock Guardrails: safeguards for generative AI applications.
- Amazon Bedrock evaluations: compare models on accuracy, robustness and toxicity.

AWS describes responsible AI dimensions including fairness, explainability, privacy and security, safety, controllability, veracity and robustness, governance and transparency.

Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/sagemaker/latest/dg/clarify-detect-data-bias.html
commonMistakes: Using Ground Truth (training labels) where A2I (reviewing live predictions) is needed.
Expecting Guardrails to measure bias in a tabular model.

title: Legal risks and responsible model choices
body:
Legal and business risks of generative AI: intellectual property infringement claims, biased outputs, hallucinations, loss of customer trust and harm to end users.

Responsible model selection weighs environmental cost too: choose the smallest model that meets the requirement, avoid unnecessary retraining, and prefer efficient hardware.

Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/aws-certification/latest/ai-practitioner-01/ai-practitioner-01-domain4.html
commonMistakes: Thinking a bigger model is the responsible default.
Treating generated content as automatically free of IP risk.

title: Transparent and explainable models
body:
- Transparent (interpretable) models, such as linear models and decision trees, show how they reach a decision.
- Black-box models, such as deep neural networks, need post-hoc explanation (for example, SHAP feature attributions from SageMaker Clarify).
- Trade-off: more complex models are often more accurate but harder to explain.

Documentation supports transparency: Amazon SageMaker Model Cards record intended use, risk rating, training details and evaluation results. Human-centered design gives users clear reasons and a way to give feedback.

Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/sagemaker/latest/dg/model-cards.html
commonMistakes: Equating high accuracy with transparency.
Using Model Registry (versions and approvals) as the documentation record.

title: Shared responsibility and data protection for AI
body:
AWS secures the cloud: facilities, hardware and the infrastructure behind services like Amazon Bedrock. The customer secures what it does in the cloud: IAM permissions, the data it sends and stores, encryption settings, network design and how the application uses model output.

Amazon Bedrock does not use customer prompts and responses to improve base models and does not share them with model providers. Data is encrypted in transit and at rest, optionally with customer managed AWS KMS keys.

Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/security.html
commonMistakes: Thinking the customer patches the hosts behind a managed service.
Believing prompts are shared with the model provider by default.

title: Securing AI workloads on AWS
body:
- IAM: least-privilege policies that control who can invoke which models.
- AWS PrivateLink: an interface VPC endpoint keeps traffic to Amazon Bedrock off the internet. (Gateway endpoints exist only for Amazon S3 and DynamoDB.)
- AWS KMS: encryption keys for data at rest.
- Amazon Macie: discovers sensitive data such as PII in Amazon S3.
- Amazon GuardDuty: threat detection. Amazon Inspector: vulnerability scanning.
- Amazon Bedrock Guardrails: filter prompts and responses, including PII masking and prompt attacks.

Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/vpc-interface-endpoints.html
commonMistakes: Creating a gateway endpoint for Bedrock: Bedrock uses an interface endpoint.
Using GuardDuty or Inspector to find PII in S3: that is Macie.

title: Governance and audit services
body:
- AWS CloudTrail: who called which API, when, from where.
- Amazon Bedrock model invocation logging: full prompts and responses to Amazon S3 or CloudWatch Logs.
- AWS Config: records resource configurations and evaluates them against rules over time.
- AWS Artifact: AWS's compliance reports (SOC, ISO) and agreements.
- AWS Audit Manager: collects evidence about your own controls.
- AWS Trusted Advisor: best-practice checks.
- Amazon Inspector: vulnerability scanning.

Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/model-invocation-logging.html
commonMistakes: Expecting CloudTrail to hold full prompt and response text.
Looking for AWS's audit reports in Audit Manager instead of Artifact.

title: Data governance for AI
body:
- Lineage: record which data, steps and jobs produced each model (Amazon SageMaker ML Lineage Tracking).
- Cataloging: describe datasets so they can be found and governed (AWS Glue Data Catalog).
- Residency: keep data and processing in approved locations. Amazon Bedrock geographic cross-Region inference keeps processing within a geography such as the EU; global cross-Region inference can route worldwide.
- Retention and logging: decide how long prompts, responses and training data are kept, and log access.
- Review cadence: revisit policies and models on a schedule.

Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/sagemaker/latest/dg/lineage-tracking.html
commonMistakes: Using a global cross-Region profile under an EU-only residency rule.
Expecting Model Cards to record lineage automatically as jobs run.

title: Generative AI Security Scoping Matrix
body:
A framework that sorts generative AI uses by how much of the stack you own, which sets your security responsibilities:

- Scope 1, consumer app: using a public generative AI service.
- Scope 2, enterprise app: using a third-party business application with generative AI features.
- Scope 3, pre-trained models: building your own application on an existing foundation model (for example, through the Amazon Bedrock API, with or without RAG).
- Scope 4, fine-tuned models: fine-tuning an existing model with your data.
- Scope 5, self-trained models: training your own model from scratch.

Read more: https://aws.amazon.com/ai/security/generative-ai-scoping-matrix/
commonMistakes: Placing a RAG application in Scope 4: retrieval does not change the model.
Placing your own application built on Bedrock in Scope 2.

title: The foundation model lifecycle
body:
A foundation model moves through these stages:

- Data selection: gather and curate the data for pre-training (model builder) or customization (you).
- Model selection: pick a model by task, modality, quality on your tests, cost, latency and compliance.
- Pre-training: the provider trains the model on very large unlabeled datasets; this is rarely repeated by a user.
- Fine-tuning or other customization: adapt the model to your task with your own data.
- Evaluation: test against representative cases and success criteria before release.
- Deployment: serve the model, for example on demand in Amazon Bedrock or on a SageMaker AI endpoint.
- Feedback: production ratings and errors drive the next round of prompt, data or tuning changes, then re-evaluation.

Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/wellarchitected/latest/generative-ai-lens/generative-ai-lifecycle.html
commonMistakes: Putting user feedback before deployment: it comes from a model people are already using.
Treating pre-training as something each customer does: it is the provider's step, before fine-tuning.

title: Context engineering
body:
Context engineering is choosing and shaping everything a model sees in one request, within its context window: system instructions, retrieved passages, memory, tool definitions and results, and conversation history.

- Models are stateless: a chat app re-sends history as input tokens, so cost and latency grow every turn.
- Keep history in budget: a sliding window drops old turns; summarizing keeps their key facts in fewer tokens.
- Retrieve only relevant chunks rather than whole documents.
- Store durable facts, such as user preferences, in long-term memory and inject only the relevant ones.
- Put static content first and changing content last, so prompt caching can reuse the prefix.

Read more: https://strandsagents.com/latest/documentation/docs/user-guide/concepts/agents/conversation-management/
commonMistakes: Raising maximum output tokens to fit a long history: it caps the reply, not the input.
Putting a timestamp or the user question at the start of a prompt and expecting cache hits.

title: Multi-agent patterns and protocols
body:
When one agent has too many tools or roles, split the work:

- Supervisor (agents as tools): a supervisor routes each request to specialist agents with narrow roles and small toolsets. Amazon Bedrock multi-agent collaboration works this way.
- Swarm: specialist agents hand tasks to each other; the path is emergent.
- Graph: a flowchart of agents where a model decision at each node picks the next step, with branches and loops.
- Workflow: a fixed, developer-defined task graph, with independent steps in parallel; the same sequence every run.

Protocols: MCP connects an agent to tools and data sources. Agent2Agent (A2A) lets independent agents, often run by different teams, exchange tasks and results.

Read more: https://strandsagents.com/latest/documentation/docs/user-guide/concepts/multi-agent/multi-agent-patterns/
commonMistakes: Choosing a swarm for a process auditors need to see run identically each time.
Using MCP to describe agent-to-agent delegation: that is A2A.

title: Amazon Bedrock AgentCore services
body:
AgentCore runs agents built with any framework (Strands Agents, LangGraph, CrewAI and others) and any model, with no infrastructure to manage. Its modular services:

- Runtime: serverless hosting for agents and tools, with session isolation.
- Memory: short-term memory for turns within a session; long-term memory for facts and preferences across sessions.
- Gateway: turns APIs and Lambda functions into MCP tools, and connects existing MCP servers.
- Identity: agent identities and credentials, including OAuth access to other services on a user's behalf.
- Code Interpreter and Browser: sandboxed tools to run code and use websites.
- Observability: traces, metrics and logs of agent behavior.

Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock-agentcore/latest/devguide/what-is-bedrock-agentcore.html
commonMistakes: Expecting short-term memory to remember a user in a new session weeks later.
Rebuilding a working LangGraph or Strands agent as a Bedrock agent just to host it: Runtime hosts it as is.

title: Amazon Quick, Kiro, Strands Agents and PartyRock
body:
- Amazon Quick: a fully managed AI workspace for business users. Chat agents answer from connected data (Quick Index), Quick Research writes cited reports, Quick Sight covers dashboards, and Quick Flows and Quick Automate automate tasks. It evolved from Amazon QuickSight.
- Kiro: an AI development environment (IDE, CLI, web). Specs turn an idea into requirements, design and tasks; steering files hold project conventions; hooks automate actions.
- Strands Agents: an open-source SDK, first released by AWS, for writing agents in a few lines with a model-first agent loop; supports Amazon Bedrock and other providers, MCP and multi-agent patterns.
- PartyRock: a no-code generative AI playground for learning and building small apps in the browser.

Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/quick/latest/userguide/what-is.html
commonMistakes: Picking AgentCore when business users want a ready-made assistant: AgentCore is for developers running their own agents.
Calling Strands Agents a hosting service: it is the SDK; AgentCore Runtime can host what you build with it.

title: Amazon Bedrock service tiers and cost levers
body:
On-demand requests can choose a service tier with the service_tier parameter:

- Standard (default): consistent performance for everyday tasks.
- Priority: fastest responses, served ahead of other tiers, for a premium; no reservation.
- Flex: a discount for workloads that tolerate longer processing, such as evaluations and summarization.
- Reserved: tokens-per-minute capacity reserved for 1 or 3 months, billed monthly, for mission-critical traffic; overflow goes to Standard.

Other levers: batch inference for asynchronous jobs, Provisioned Throughput for model units by the hour, intelligent prompt routing between models in a family, distillation to a smaller model, and Custom Model Import to serve your own weights on demand.

Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/service-tiers-inference.html
commonMistakes: Choosing Flex for a latency-sensitive app: Flex trades speed for price.
Reserving capacity around the clock for traffic that peaks only a few hours a day.

title: Choosing a foundation model for an application
body:
Match the model to the application before comparing price:

- Modality: what goes in and what comes out (text, image, video, audio, embeddings). A photo-plus-question app needs a multimodal model that accepts images.
- Input and output length: the context window caps the tokens in one request; the maximum output setting caps the reply.
- Latency and model size: smaller models answer faster and cost less per token. Pick the smallest model that passes your own evaluation.
- Languages, customization options (fine-tuning, distillation) and Region availability.
- Cost: price per input and output token. Prompt caching cuts the cost and latency of a long prefix that repeats across requests.

Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/nova/latest/userguide/what-is-nova.html
commonMistakes: Raising the maximum output tokens to fit a long document: the context window limits the input.
Choosing an image generation model to read photos: reading images needs a multimodal model that accepts image input.

title: Vector stores for embeddings on AWS
body:
A vector store keeps embeddings and finds the ones nearest to a query vector (similarity search). It is the retrieval step of RAG.

- Amazon OpenSearch Serverless and Amazon OpenSearch Service: search engines with vector search, for frequent low-latency queries.
- Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL and Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL: the pgvector extension stores vectors beside relational data.
- Amazon Neptune Analytics: graph plus vector search. It powers GraphRAG in Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases, which links entities across documents.
- Amazon S3 Vectors: low-cost, durable vector storage in S3 with sub-second queries, best for large, infrequently queried data.

Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/knowledge-base-setup.html
commonMistakes: Picking a time-series or key-value database for similarity search: it needs vector search support.
Expecting bigger chunks to answer questions that link entities across documents: that is a GraphRAG job.

title: Agents, workflows and their business uses
body:
- AI agent: a model plans the steps toward a goal, calls tools such as APIs, keeps memory and decides when it is done. It fits open-ended tasks that act in other systems: rebooking travel, processing a refund, triaging IT tickets.
- Workflow: a fixed sequence of steps defined in advance. Amazon Bedrock Flows links prompts, models, knowledge bases and other AWS services into such a sequence, so every run follows the same auditable path.
- A single model call is enough for one-step tasks such as translation, summarization or classification.

Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/flows.html
commonMistakes: Using an agent where the steps never change: a workflow is cheaper and more predictable.
Building an agent for a task that is one request and one response.

title: Prompt templates and versions in Amazon Bedrock Prompt Management
body:
Prompt Management stores prompts with their model and inference settings so teams can share and reuse them.

- Variables turn a stored prompt into a reusable template that the application fills in at run time.
- While testing, compare variants of a prompt and keep the one with the best output.
- Saving edits updates the working draft.
- Creating a version takes a snapshot of the prompt. Applications call a specific version, so draft edits reach production only after a new version is created and the application points at it.
- To roll back, point the application at an earlier version.

Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/prompt-management-deploy.html
commonMistakes: Expecting a draft edit to change what production returns: production calls a saved version.
Using a model registry to version prompts: it versions models.

title: Preparing data to fine-tune a foundation model
body:
- Format: in Amazon Bedrock, training and validation sets are .jsonl files; for supervised fine-tuning each record pairs a prompt with its expected completion.
- Curation: quality beats volume. Remove duplicates, errors and off-task examples.
- Governance: detect and redact personal data (for example with Amazon Comprehend) and confirm the right to use the data before training.
- Representativeness: cover every kind of input, user group and market the model will serve.
- Size and validation: hold out a validation set. Training loss falling while validation loss rises means overfitting.
- Labels: supervised and instruction fine-tuning need labeled pairs; RLHF uses human preferences between responses to train a reward model; reinforcement fine-tuning uses reward functions instead of labels.

Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/model-customization-prepare.html
commonMistakes: Encrypting a dataset and calling it governed: the model still trains on the personal data inside.
Reading falling training loss alone as success: check validation loss for overfitting.

title: Evaluating GenAI applications and their business value
body:
Evaluate the whole application, not only the model:

- RAG: Amazon Bedrock RAG evaluations run retrieve-only jobs (are the right passages returned?) or retrieve-and-generate jobs (are the answers good too?).
- Agents: score the trajectory as well as the reply. Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Evaluations scores agent traces for goal attainment and tool use with LLM-as-a-judge evaluators.
- Custom rules: a judge-model evaluation job with a custom metric scores business-specific criteria without reference answers.
- Business alignment: task completion rate, user satisfaction, cost per interaction, time saved (productivity) and user engagement.

Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/evaluation-kb.html
commonMistakes: Judging an agent on its final text alone: wrong tool calls can hide behind a plausible reply.
Reporting ROUGE or perplexity when leadership asks about business value.

title: The dimensions of responsible AI
body:
AWS describes responsible AI through these dimensions:

- Fairness: considering impacts on different groups of stakeholders.
- Explainability: understanding and evaluating system outputs.
- Privacy and security: appropriately obtaining, using and protecting data and models.
- Safety: preventing harmful system output and misuse.
- Controllability: having mechanisms to monitor and steer AI system behavior.
- Veracity and robustness: achieving correct system outputs, even with unexpected or adversarial inputs.
- Governance: incorporating best practices into the AI supply chain, including providers and deployers.
- Transparency: enabling stakeholders to make informed choices about their engagement with an AI system.

Inclusivity sits close to fairness: the system and its data should serve every group of users it is meant for.

Read more: https://aws.amazon.com/ai/responsible-ai/
commonMistakes: Filing wrong answers on typos or odd phrasing under fairness: correct output on unexpected input is veracity and robustness.
Confusing transparency (informing stakeholders about the system) with explainability (understanding a given output).

title: Human-centered design for explainable AI
body:
Explanations are built for the people who receive the decision, not only for the model's builders:

- AI decision transparency: tell users when AI is involved and show the main factors behind a decision, in language they can follow, with a confidence level where it helps.
- Guidance on trust: help users see when to rely on an output, when to verify it and when to override it.
- User-feedback mechanisms: let users rate, report or challenge an output, and feed what they report back into improving the system.
- Recourse: give people affected by a decision a way to contest it and reach a human reviewer.

Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/wellarchitected/latest/responsible-ai-lens/raiuc04-bp01.html
commonMistakes: Treating an overall accuracy figure as an explanation of one person's decision.
Publishing model weights or code to end users and calling that explainable.

title: AI Service Cards, open models and licenses
body:
Where to find out how a model was built and what it is for:

- AWS AI Service Cards: AWS's own documentation of an AWS AI service's intended use cases and limitations, responsible AI design choices and performance best practices.
- Amazon SageMaker Model Cards: your documentation of the models you build.
- Open-weight models: the weights and architecture can be inspected, which helps audits, but the training data may be only partly described.
- Licenses: models in Amazon SageMaker JumpStart come under licenses chosen by their providers (for example Apache 2.0 or Responsible AI Licenses), and some require accepting an end-user license agreement. Review the terms before you build a product on a model.

Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/sagemaker/latest/dg/jumpstart-foundation-models-choose.html
commonMistakes: Assuming publicly available weights allow any commercial use.
Looking in SageMaker Model Cards for AWS's documentation of its managed AI services.
